name: Michoacán Nahuatl
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Sischo, William R. 1979. 'Michoacan Nahual', in Langacker (ed.), Modern Aztec Grammatical Sketches (SIL Publications in Linguistics 56:2); series confirmed on archive.org but Michoacan chapter not openly readable.

new_statements.quote: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable except in verbals in which the final two syllables are contracted into one syllable, and then the stress falls on the ultimate syllable. It is usual for speakers to say the contracted form: tomáwak → tomák 'fat'; úyak → úk 'he went'; nimicmáka → nimicmá 'I give it to you'. There are also some locative words with ultimate stress that is invariable, but through comparison with words in other dialects they are found to be probable contractions of two syllables originally. One can only guess at the sounds that were dropped: *lasiwakan, *lasiwayan (?) now always heard as lasiwán 'shade'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable. Surface final stress arises only where the last two syllables have contracted into one (very common in verb forms: tomáwak > tomák, nimicmáka > nimicmá), i.e. stress stays on the vowel that was penultimate before contraction; a handful of locative nouns (lasiwán 'shade') have lexicalised final stress explained as old contractions. The 2015 Spanish grammar by the same author restates the rule: 'Ordinariamente, el acento en náhuatl cae en la penúltima sílaba. Cuando la penúltima sílaba se contrae con la última sílaba, el acento cae en la última y se escribe con el acento ortográfico. Ejemplo: chicahuac (fuerte, duro); chicác.' (Sischo & Erickson de Hollenbach 2015, Gramática breve del náhuatl de Michoacán, sec. 2, p.3; file).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in either source (Gordon 2023 cites Sischo 1979 among Nahuatl descriptions reporting a single stress per word).
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Contracted verbals: final two syllables fuse and stress surfaces on the final syllable (tomák, úk, nimicmá; 2015: chicác, xiyén < xiyecan); (ii) a few locative words with invariable final stress, taken to be historical contractions (lasiwán 'shade'; 2015 Vocabulario: ilasehuán, amalá). The 2015 orthography marks these with a written accent, and also writes an accent on the penult when the final syllable is a bare vowel (panúa).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated for the word in general (citation/isolated forms and text examples); contraction-induced final stress applies across word classes but is described as typical of verb forms. Unstressed-vowel effects (i~e, u~o fluctuation; final unstressed a raised) are keyed to this word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Both primary sources describe the speech of Pómaro (municipio de Aquila, coastal Michoacán), the reference variety of Glottolog mich1245 / ISO ncl ('Michoacán Nahual' in SIL usage; 1979 also names Ostula, Coire and San Pedro Naranjestil as villages of the dialect). sources.note: p.312 (Phonology): 'Stress falls on the penultimate syllable except in verbals in which the final two syllables are contracted into one syllable, and then the stress falls on the ultimate syllable' (tomáwak > tomák, úyak > úk, nimicmáka > nimicmá); also a few locative words with invariable final stress, analysed as old contractions (lasiwán 'shade'). Also notes vowel raising/fluctuation in unstressed syllables and w-loss after a stressed front-vowel syllable.

sources.note: Sec. 2 'El alfabeto y las reglas morfofonémicas', p.3: 'Ordinariamente, el acento en náhuatl cae en la penúltima sílaba. Cuando la penúltima sílaba se contrae con la última sílaba, el acento cae en la última y se escribe con el acento ortográfico. Ejemplo: chicahuac (fuerte, duro); chicác.' Written accent also used on a penult when the final syllable is a lone vowel (panúa). p.2: unstressed i/e and u/o neutralise. Copula section: xiyecan > xiyén, 'al perder las letras -ca-, el acento se pasa a la última sílaba'.
